title: Computer-Aided Design (CAD)
summary: Parametric 3D modeling, wireframe/surface/solid paradigms, assemblies, drawings, and STEP/IGES data exchange.

sections.heading: What Is CAD?
sections.content: **Computer-Aided Design (CAD)** is the use of software to create, modify, analyze, and document engineering geometry. CAD replaced the manual drafting board and is now the master repository of product geometry: every downstream consumer — drawings, [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]] callouts, [[cae-analysis|simulation]], [[cam-computer-aided-manufacturing|CAM]], and inspection — reads from the CAD model.

sections.heading: 2D Drafting vs. 3D Modeling
sections.content:
**2D CAD** produces orthographic drawings directly — views, dimensions, title blocks. It is fast for simple flat parts but error-prone because geometry exists only as lines.

**3D CAD** builds a solid model once, then derives 2D drawings from it automatically, which guarantees views agree with each other. Modern practice is *model-centric*: design in 3D, derive drawings, and share the 3D file for simulation and manufacturing. 2D remains essential at the inspection and shop-floor level.

sections.heading: Wireframe, Surface & Solid Modeling
sections.content:
| Paradigm | Geometry | Best For | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Wireframe** | Edges only (lines/arcs) | Simple layouts, math definitions | No faces — ambiguous, cannot shade |
| **Surface** | Bounded faces (NURBS patches) | Aerodynamic bodies, consumer shells | No enclosed volume by itself |
| **Solid** | Closed volume (B-rep / CSG) | Machined parts, mass properties | Complex freeform shapes are hard |

Most production design is **solid modeling** with surface features for freeform regions. **Hybrid modeling** mixes both.

Mathematically, freeform curves and surfaces are built from **Bézier** or **NURBS** (Non-Uniform Rational B-Spline) representations:

$$B(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} (1-t)^{n-i} t^i P_i$$

where $P_i$ are control points and $t \in [0,1]$ parameterizes the curve.

sections.heading: Parametric & Feature-Based Modeling
sections.content:
Modern CAD is **parametric**: geometry is driven by dimensions and relationships that can be edited. A **feature tree** (history tree) records the construction sequence — sketch, extrude, fillet, hole, pattern — and any dimension or feature can be edited later to regenerate the model.

Design intent is captured through:
- **Constraints** — coincident, parallel, tangent, concentric
- **Equations & global variables** — e.g., wall thickness = 0.1 × overall length
- **Design tables / configurations** — families of parts from one base model

This is what makes engineering changes cheap: edit one number, and the whole model (and its drawings) updates consistently.

sections.heading: Assemblies & Constraints
sections.content:
An **assembly** positions multiple parts relative to each other using **mates/constraints**: coincident, concentric, distance, angle, tangent. A fully constrained assembly leaves **zero degrees of freedom** and matches the intended mechanism behavior.

Assembly analysis includes:
- **Interference detection** — find overlapping solids before manufacturing
- **Motion studies** — simulate linkages and mechanisms
- **Bill of Materials (BOM)** — automatic parts lists for purchasing
- **Tolerance analysis** — stack-up of [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]] tolerances across the assembly

sections.heading: Drawings & GD&T Integration
sections.content:
Drawings are the legal communication between design and the shop floor. Derived views (front, section, detail, isometric) are projected automatically from the 3D model, and dimensions plus [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]] feature control frames are applied per **ASME Y14.5**.

Modern practice embeds the GD&T tolerance data digitally (PMI — Product and Manufacturing Information) so downstream inspection and [[cae-analysis|CAE]] can consume the same tolerance model used on the drawing.

sections.heading: File Formats & Data Exchange
sections.content:
Not every CAD system speaks the same format. Neutral exchange formats break vendor lock-in:

| Format | Type | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| **STEP (.stp)** | ISO 10303 solid | The industry-standard exchange format |
| **IGES (.igs)** | Legacy surface/curve | Older systems, surface data |
| **STL** | Triangle mesh | 3D printing, visualization |
| **Parasolid / ACIS** | Kernel formats | Native exchange between kernel partners |
| **DXF/DWG** | 2D drawing | Shop-floor drawings, laser/waterjet cutting |

Rule of thumb: use STEP for solids, STL for printing, DXF for 2D cutting — and always check tolerance and units after conversion.

keyTakeaways: The 3D model is the single source of truth; drawings are derived views of it.
Parametric, feature-based modeling makes engineering changes cheap and consistent.
Solid modeling covers most machined parts; surface/NURBS handles freeform aesthetics.
Mates/constraints fully define assemblies and enable interference and motion checks.
STEP is the default neutral exchange format for transferring solid geometry between systems.
